primary.title: Same-day future events are counted as missed before they start
primary.evidence: Both aggregates select required events using only `.lte("date", "now()")` or `.lte("date", today)`. Missing attendance then becomes `missed = total_required - attended - excused`; one miss is enough for `warning` and three for `delinquent`.
primary.current_behavior: At midnight, every required event scheduled later that day enters attendance and standing denominators. Members without early check-ins or approved excuses are immediately treated as absent.
primary.why_it_matters: Standing can deteriorate before members have had an opportunity to attend, and attendance percentages shown during the day are false.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. Schedule three required events for 8 PM today. 2. At 9 AM, request standings. 3. Every member without attendance rows has three unexcused absences. 4. `derive_standing` returns `delinquent` before any event begins.
primary.blast_radius: Every required event on its calendar date, affecting chapter-wide attendance summaries, engagement scores, and standing.
primary.tests_detect: No. `tests/events/test_attendance_summary.py` covers prior days and a future day, but no event later on the current day.

primary.title: Ambiguous attendance-session bindings fail open and can extend public check-in beyond closes_at
primary.evidence: `_session_for_link` returns `None` when more than one session is bound to a link. `validate_checkin_link` applies `closes_at` only `if session`. Creating a short-link session first creates a link and binds all open unbound sessions, then inserts another session pointing at that same link. Neither table has a cardinality constraint for one active link per event or one session per link.
primary.current_behavior: An open manual session followed by a short-link session can produce two sessions bound to one link. The validator treats that as ambiguous and skips the session close gate, leaving the public link valid until its independent TTL. Concurrent link creation can also leave multiple active links for one event because deactivation and insertion are separate autocommit transactions.
primary.why_it_matters: Members can check in after an officer-defined session closes, and officers may see or distribute competing active codes. This corrupts the attendance record used by standing and fines.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. Create an open manual attendance session for an event. 2. Create a short-link session for the same event. 3. Link creation binds the manual session, then session creation inserts a second bound session. 4. Let both `closes_at` values pass. 5. Submit the public code; `_session_for_link` returns `None`, so validation accepts it until link TTL.
primary.blast_radius: Events using attendance sessions, particularly those mixing manual and short-link/QR modes; concurrent officers opening links are also affected.
primary.tests_detect: Partial. `tests/attendance/test_checkin_links_unit.py` expects ambiguity to return `None` and separately tests one closed bound session, but never verifies that ambiguous bindings fail closed. `tests/attendance/test_checkin_flow.py` covers sequential link operations only.
primary.recommendation: Move link/session creation into one locked RPC. Add a partial unique index for one active link per event and a uniqueness/cardinality rule for `attendance_sessions.checkin_link_id`. Treat multiple bound sessions as invalid/fail-closed, and apply the same session gate to active-link reads.

primary.title: An approved excuse and an event fine can both stand, and nothing in the database stops a second fine for the same event and member
primary.evidence: at_set_attendance on status 'excused' deletes and reinserts an approved excuse and does not call tr_void_invoice (0146:186-191). at_review_excuse voids at most one row: SELECT id ... AND status = 'unpaid' LIMIT 1 (0146:278-288). unpaid_invoices has only a non-unique index on source_event_id (0010:28-29). issue_fines skips a member only after a Python read of existing kind='fine' rows, including cancelled ones (fines_legacy.py:65-73, 200-202). POST /api/treasury/invoices accepts kind/source 'fine' with an arbitrary amount and no event, 24h, or excuse check (invoices.py:36-44, 78-94).
primary.current_behavior: The manual issue path (POST /api/fines/issue) refuses members who are checked in or have an approved excuse, and uses idempotency key fine:{event}:{member} on tr_create_invoice_v2. Marking attendance excused writes the approved excuse and leaves every fine invoice in place. Excuse review voids one unpaid fine and leaves partially_paid fines and any second unpaid fine. Check-in upserts checked_in=true and does not void a fine. There is no unique index on (source_event_id, member_id) for live fines, and tr_create_invoice / tr_create_invoice_v2 do not look at attendance or excuses. A generic invoice create can insert kind='fine' with no source event.
primary.why_it_matters: Standing and the member's balance both treat an unpaid kind='fine' invoice as money owed. The product rule that an excused member is not fined is true only for the review-excuse path, and only for a single unpaid invoice. Two issuance RPCs (tr_create_invoice from process_event_fines with a null idempotency key, and tr_create_invoice_v2 from issue_fines) do not share a key, so a race or a second caller inserts a second fine that review will not fully clear.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. Treasurer POST /api/fines/issue for member M on required event E after the 24h gate; tr_create_invoice_v2 inserts an unpaid $25 fine. 2. Officer POST /api/attendance/event/E/manual/M with status excused; at_set_attendance inserts an approved excuse and does not void the invoice. 3. M now has an approved excuse and an unpaid fine; standing still counts UNPAID_FINES. 4. Separately, two concurrent POST /api/fines/process-event/E calls both pass the read-then-write dedup in process_event_fines (null idempotency key) and insert two fines; PUT /api/excuses/{id}/review voids only the first unpaid row.
primary.blast_radius: Every required-event fine, standing, and the member balance cache for that invoice. Waiving via the treasurer void route still works; the attendance-excused path does not.
primary.tests_detect: partial. tests/attendance/test_tenant_guards.py::test_approve_after_fine_processing_voids_the_invoice covers at_review_excuse on one unpaid invoice. No test asserts at_set_attendance excused voids a fine, that partially_paid fines are voided, or that a unique constraint blocks a second fine.
primary.recommendation: Add a partial unique index on unpaid_invoices (source_event_id, member_id) WHERE kind='fine' AND status <> 'cancelled'. Call the same void used by at_review_excuse from the excused branch of at_set_attendance, and void every open (unpaid or partially_paid) fine for that pair. Keep the 24h and audience checks, but do not rely on a prior SELECT for uniqueness.

primary.title: Unused setup and reset codes stay valid after password changes and do not revoke the current session
primary.evidence: redeem_setup_code loads token_version, then calls au_consume_setup_code, then mints with the pre-read version: api/auth/api/auth.py:466-468 `_issue_member_token(member["id"], member.get("token_version"))`. au_set_password only updates password_hash and token_version (migrations/0148_auth_hardening.sql:129-132) and does not touch member_setup_codes. au_consume_setup_code marks one row used and flips invited→active; it does not bump token_version or expire sibling codes (0148:187-205). issue_reset_code inserts a new code via _issue_setup_code and only then bumps the epoch (auth.py:498-508). Redeem selects the 10 newest codes (auth.py:431-436) but does not invalidate the rest.
primary.current_behavior: A setup or reset code is a bearer credential for 7 days. Setting a password bumps token_version and kills JWTs minted earlier, but every still-unused code remains redeemable. Redemption mints a JWT at the member's current token_version and leaves other live sessions in place. Issuing a reset does not burn older unused codes. An officer with members:invite (the officer role has that key since migration 0147) receives the plaintext code in the HTTP body as well as email.
primary.why_it_matters: token_version is the only server-side revocation control. An unused code is a second login that ignores it, so a password change does not close a code that was already issued, and redeeming that code does not kick the legitimate session.

Victim POST /api/auth/login with their password, then POST /api/auth/set-password → token_version N+1; the reset code row is still used_at NULL. 3. Holder of the code POST /api/auth/redeem-setup-code {email, code} → 200 access_token whose ver equals N+1. 4. GET /api/auth/me with that token is the victim; the victim's post-password token still works until someone bumps the epoch again. The same sequence works for any unused invite code that was not the one the member redeemed.

Parallel access for up to 7 days after the member believes they recovered the account. Officers can mint these codes for anyone in the chapter.
primary.tests_detect: no. tests/auth/test_tokens.py asserts a bumped ver kills old JWTs. tests/auth/test_invite_setup_codes.py asserts reset bumps token_version and that the new code redeems. Neither redeems a leftover code after set-password, nor checks that sibling codes are burned.

primary.title: Failed setup/reset rows retain plaintext credentials indefinitely and Retry ignores credential expiry
primary.evidence: The plaintext code is placed in `message_outbox.payload`. `_close_row` wipes it only for `sent` or `simulated`; comments explicitly preserve failed payloads for Retry. `retry_outbox_row` checks only `status == 'failed'`, and the template renders the code without validating `expires_at`. Repository-wide search found no retention or cleanup path for failed outbox payloads.
primary.current_behavior: A failed row stores a live code for up to seven days and retains it after expiry indefinitely. An officer can later retry it, causing an expired or already-used code to be emailed. The officer UI hides the body, but the plaintext remains in the database.
primary.why_it_matters: This expands credential exposure from one-time issuance to durable database storage and sends confusing invalid credentials during recovery. A database read compromise during the validity window reveals usable setup/reset codes.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. An officer issues a reset code. 2. SMTP is unavailable, so the row fails and keeps the plaintext. 3. The member redeems the code through another channel, or seven days pass. 4. An officer retries the failed row. 5. The drain emails the obsolete code and only then wipes the payload.
primary.blast_radius: All failed SETUP_CODE and RESET_CODE messages.
primary.tests_detect: partial — tests/cron/test_drain_email.py::test_a_failed_setup_code_row_keeps_its_payload explicitly verifies retention, and sent/simulated wiping is covered. No test covers expiry, redemption, cleanup, or Retry of an obsolete code.
primary.recommendation: Store an encrypted delivery artifact or regenerate a fresh code on retry. Add an expiry check before rendering, terminally redact expired/used credentials, and enforce a retention policy for failed secret-bearing rows.

primary.title: Autocommitted Python workflows leave event and attendance state half-applied
primary.evidence: Every builder execution sets `conn.autocommit = True` (`postgres.py:169-186`). `update_event` commits the event update at `events.py:574-581` before calling `ev_set_audience` at `583-594`. `create_checkin_link` first deactivates every active link (`checkin_links.py:178-182`) and only then attempts the replacement insert (`184-203`). `create_session` creates the link, reads it back, inserts a session, and finally updates the event pointer as four separately committed operations (`sessions.py:38-68`). Outbox retry similarly requeues first and audits second (`outbox.py:157-169`).
primary.current_behavior: A later validation, insert, audit, or database failure does not roll back earlier steps. `create_session` also calls a helper that acquires its own global `get_db()` client rather than using the supplied client, making an encompassing transaction impossible.
primary.why_it_matters: These are state-machine transitions whose intermediate states are observable: updated visibility with an old audience, no active check-in link, an orphan active link, an unpointed session, or a requeued message without its required audit.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. An officer updates an event and supplies a custom audience. 2. The scalar event update commits. 3. `ev_set_audience` rejects one cross-chapter member or the DB connection fails. 4. The API errors, but the title/time/visibility remains changed and the old audience remains. A parallel sequence can deactivate the only check-in link before the replacement insert fails.
primary.blast_radius: Individual events, attendance sessions, active door links, and retried messages; concurrent users can act on the intermediate state.

primary.recommendation: Implement `ev_update_event`, attendance-session creation/link rotation, and outbox retry as transactional RPCs. At minimum, pass one explicit transaction-capable client through helpers and add phase-by-phase failure tests.

primary.evidence: `dispatch_send` selects rows where `status = 'pending'` at api/announcements/services/sms.py:232-239 and sends them without first changing their status. The cron path atomically changes pending rows to `sending` through `outbox_claim_batch`, whose SQL uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` at migrations/0155_outbox_claim.sql:109-123. Both announcement and event request handlers immediately invoke the unclaimed dispatcher after their RPC.

primary.title: Provider success is committed before delivery state, allowing retries to duplicate real messages
primary.evidence: The cron calls `twilio_client.send_sms(...)` or `send_email(...)` before `_close_row(... status='sent')` at api/cron/services/outbox_drain.py:227-228 and 247-248. `_deliver_row` explicitly leaves a row in `sending` when bookkeeping fails, and the migration requeues it after 15 minutes. Twilio returns a SID, but line 65 says callers ignore it; no provider identifier is persisted.
primary.current_behavior: External delivery and local acknowledgement are two separate, non-idempotent operations. A successful provider request followed by a database failure is indistinguishable from an unsent abandoned claim and is retried.
primary.why_it_matters: This is an at-least-once system presented as exactly-once. Duplicate payment, assignment, credential, or chapter-wide messages can occur during ordinary transient database failures.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. Cron claims a row. 2. Twilio or SMTP accepts and sends it. 3. The database update marking the row `sent` fails. 4. The row remains `sending`. 5. Fifteen minutes later the reaper returns it to `pending`. 6. A later cron sends the message again.

primary.title: The advertised transactional outbox is post-commit and suppresses arbitrary insert failures
primary.evidence: `create_invoice_v2` commits `tr_create_invoice_v2`, recomputes the cache, and only then calls `notify_invoice_issued` (`invoices.py:82-103`). `enqueue` catches every `Exception` from the insert and returns `None`, claiming it merely lost a UNIQUE race (`outbox.py:100-105`). `enqueue_many` likewise swallows the bulk error before retrying rows (`outbox.py:157-177`). The documentation claims the enqueue is transactional and uses `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` (`treasury/notifications.py:1-16`), but the implementation does a pre-read plus ordinary insert.
primary.current_behavior: Financial or account state can commit without a corresponding outbox row. A constraint error, missing table, connection failure, serialization issue, or pool failure is indistinguishable from a duplicate dedup key and is not logged by the shared enqueue layer.
primary.why_it_matters: A missing row cannot be recovered by the drain worker. Invoice, payment, refund, event, and setup-code messages can be permanently absent while the initiating request reports success.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. `tr_create_invoice_v2` commits the invoice, ledger, and audit rows. 2. The subsequent outbox insert fails because the connection drops or the schema is incompatible. 3. `enqueue` returns `None`. 4. The route returns the created invoice. 5. No pending message exists for cron to retry.
primary.blast_radius: All Python-enqueued email notifications, including treasury lifecycle messages, event emails, setup/reset codes, and bulk fan-out notifications.
primary.tests_detect: partial — `tests/treasury/test_chunkG_rebuild_hardening.py` tests successful persistence and duplicate deduplication; `tests/auth/test_code_emails.py` tests a wrapper logging a raised enqueue error. Neither test injects a non-UNIQUE failure inside `api.platform.outbox.enqueue`, where the exception is swallowed.
primary.recommendation: Move business-state and outbox insertion into the same RPC transaction. Where that is not immediately possible, use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (dedup_key) DO NOTHING RETURNING *`, suppress only `UniqueViolation`, log/raise every other error, and add failure-injection tests.

primary.title: A one-cent partial payment clears standing, because engagement counts only status='unpaid' fines at face value

primary.title: Invoice coverage is stored two ways, and reallocating a payment that still has verified_payments.invoice_id marks a second invoice paid
primary.evidence: 0031 still sets verified_payments.invoice_id and then `SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount_cents),0) INTO v_paid_sum FROM verified_payments WHERE invoice_id = v_submission.invoice_id` and `UPDATE unpaid_invoices SET status = v_new_status` with no cancelled check. 0124 remaining is `amount_cents - SUM(verified_payments.invoice_id) - tr_net_allocated_cents`. v2 inserts invoice_id NULL. tr_reallocate_payment appends allocation rows and never clears invoice_id. 0012 inserts migrated paid fines with invoice_id set and submission_id NULL. POST /api/treasury/payments/submissions/{id}/verify still calls svc.verify_payment (the 0031 RPC). POST /payments/{id}/reallocate is live for treasury:invoice:void.
primary.current_behavior: A v2 verification attributes money only through payment_allocations. A legacy verification, and every paid fine migrated by 0012, also stores coverage on verified_payments.invoice_id. Reallocating one of those payments adds allocations without removing the direct column, so tr_invoice_remaining_cents subtracts the same cents twice and tr_refresh_invoice_status can mark both the original invoice and the new target paid. Separately, legacy verify does not call tr_refresh_invoice_status: it ignores existing allocations when it writes status, and if the invoice was voided after the submission was created it overwrites status from cancelled back to partially_paid or paid.
primary.why_it_matters: BalanceEngine still counts every non-cancelled invoice in owed and every verified payment in paid, so the member's outstanding number stays honest. Invoice status does not. Open-invoice lists, fine totals, oldest-first allocation, and the SPA pay form all key off status. One historical or legacy-verified payment can make two invoices look collected.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. A paid fine was migrated by 0012, or an officer POSTs /api/treasury/payments/submissions/{id}/verify (not verify-v1) on an invoice-targeted submission. verified_payments.invoice_id = invoice A, A.status = paid. 2. Treasurer POSTs /api/treasury/payments/{vp}/reallocate with allocations [{invoice_id: B, amount_cents: A's amount}] and a reason. 3. No prior allocation rows exist, so nothing is reversed. A new allocation lands on B. remaining(A) = amount - direct - 0 = 0 (stays paid). remaining(B) = amount - 0 - allocation = 0 (becomes paid). 4. owed includes A and B; paid includes the money once. outstanding equals one invoice, but neither invoice is open. 5. greekos pay proof requires an open invoice (api.submitPaymentProof); there is no balance-submission client. The member still owes and the UI has nothing to pay. Alternate: submit proof, POST /invoices/{id}/void while the submission is pending, then POST the legacy verify URL. 0031 locks the cancelled invoice and writes status back to paid/partially_paid, leaving the CANCEL_INVOICE ledger row in place.
primary.blast_radius: Any chapter with a 0012 paid-fine row, or any client that still calls the legacy verify route. The current SPA calls verify-v1 only, so it does not create new invoice_id payments, but reallocate of migrated rows is one authenticated POST.
primary.tests_detect: no. tests/treasury/test_v1_allocation.py reallocates only v2 payments (invoice_id NULL) and expects the original invoice to return to unpaid. tests/treasury/test_chunkC_payments.py exercises tr_verify_payment in isolation and does not void-then-verify or reallocate a direct-linked payment.

primary.title: A refund raises what the member owes and does not reopen an invoice, and the SPA can only pay an open invoice
primary.evidence: tr_issue_refund inserts refunds status=active capped by the sum of active refunds against that verified payment, and a REFUND_ISSUED ledger row of -amount. It does not insert allocation reversals and does not call tr_refresh_invoice_status. _member_figures uses `current = owed - paid + adjustments + refunds` with refunds as a positive sum of amount_cents. chapter_balance uses `payments - expenses + chapter adjustments - refunds`. The SPA's only money-in call is submitPaymentProof, which requires an invoice_id. No greekos reference to /payments/balance-submissions or /refunds.
primary.current_behavior: The signs match: a refund reduces chapter cash and increases the member's net position back toward owing (it undoes paid, it does not also delete the payment). The invoice that the payment covered stays paid, because coverage lives in allocations / invoice_id and the refund RPC does not touch them. outstanding becomes positive with zero open invoices when that was the member's only invoice. Officer role includes treasury:refund:create (0147), so this is not treasurer-only.
primary.why_it_matters: The balance number is right and the invoice list is not. The member owes again, the chapter has less cash, and the only pay control in the product needs an open invoice. POST /api/treasury/payments/balance-submissions would accept a payment against the overall balance, but the SPA never calls it. Until someone creates a new invoice or calls that route, the refunded member cannot pay what the balance says they owe.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. Member pays a $100 invoice; verify-v1 marks it paid; outstanding 0. 2. Officer POSTs /api/treasury/refunds {verified_payment_id, amount_cents: 10000, reason}. 3. refunds row active, ledger -10000, invoice still paid. current = 10000 owed - 10000 paid + 10000 refund = 10000. 4. Member opens Finance. open_invoices is empty (status filter unpaid/partially_paid). The pay form never renders a target. 5. Chapter cash is down $100. The receivable exists only as a balance figure.
primary.blast_radius: Any refund of a payment that fully covered the member's open invoices. Partial refunds leave the same gap for the refunded slice.
primary.tests_detect: partial. tests/treasury/test_chunkE_adjustments_refunds.py asserts the cap, the negative ledger row, and the balance formula. It does not assert invoice status after a refund, and nothing in greekos asserts a way to pay a positive outstanding with no open invoice.
primary.recommendation: On refund, append allocation reversals up to the refunded amount and let tr_refresh_invoice_status reopen the invoice, or create a replacement invoice for the refunded cents inside the same RPC. Expose balance submissions in the pay UI when outstanding > 0 and open invoices are empty.

The defect is also broader than reported because `tr_issue_refund` does not restrict refunds to the member's available overpayment credit; it permits refunding funds allocated to satisfied debt.

primary.title: The tables balances are computed from can be updated in place; the append-only ledger is not what members owe
primary.evidence: _member_figures sums unpaid_invoices where status != cancelled, all verified_payments.amount_cents, active finance_adjustments.delta_cents, and active refunds.amount_cents. It never reads big_ledger. verified_payments has no UPDATE or DELETE trigger. receipts reference verified_payments with no ON DELETE clause and block UPDATE/DELETE of the receipt, so a payment row with a receipt cannot be deleted, but its amount_cents can be updated. finance_adjustments and refunds have tr_block_delete only; delta_cents, amount_cents, and status are updatable. big_ledger allows only active→invalidated, and that flip is not written to audit_logs. LedgerWriter.invalidate performs that update and is referenced only from tests.
primary.current_behavior: Application routes do not .update() these tables; money routes go through RPCs. The connection is the table owner, which bypasses RLS, and the query builder will run an UPDATE if any caller asks. Changing verified_payments.amount_cents changes outstanding and chapter cash on the next recompute, while the receipt and the PAYMENT_RECEIVED row keep the old amount. Changing finance_adjustments.delta_cents changes the member balance without a new ledger row. Rebuild would report drift after the fact. It does not prevent the write. Dropping the ledger triggers is a superuser action and is accepted; these tables do not have the triggers to drop.
primary.why_it_matters: The append-only story is true for the shadow log and false for the tables that define what a member owes. One UPDATE from the owner role, a future service bug, or a Supabase SQL editor session rewrites balances with no audit row. Invalidating a ledger row (the one mutation the trigger allows) is also unaudited, and nothing in the app records who flipped it.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. Owner session: UPDATE verified_payments SET amount_cents = amount_cents + 100000 WHERE id = <payment>. 2. Receipt row still shows the original amount (update trigger rejects a matching receipt edit). PAYMENT_RECEIVED stays at the original amount. 3. Next get_member_balance recomputes from verified_payments and drops the member's outstanding by $1000, and chapter_balance rises by $1000. 4. POST /api/treasury/rebuild reports a PAYMENT_RECEIVED count mismatch and does not change big_ledger. The new balance remains.
primary.blast_radius: All chapters, any path that can issue SQL as the pooler role. No current route does this. The gap is the integrity model, not a live handler.
primary.tests_detect: partial. tests/treasury/test_chunk0_foundations.py asserts ledger and audit immutability. tests/treasury/test_chunkG_rebuild_hardening.py asserts rebuild reports drift and does not rewrite the ledger. No test asserts that verified_payments.amount_cents or finance_adjustments.delta_cents cannot change.
primary.recommendation: Before-update triggers on verified_payments, finance_adjustments, refunds, and unpaid_invoices that allow only the column transitions the RPCs actually perform (invoice status, adjustment pending→active, expense active→invalidated, submission pending→approved/rejected). Point balance reads at those guarded rows knowing the amounts are frozen. Audit the ledger active→invalidated transition inside tr_enforce_big_ledger_update.

findings.corrections: The balance citation must extend through api/treasury/core/balance.py:142, not :102, because the adjustment/refund helpers are part of the calculation. Rebuild does not merely report a generic PAYMENT_RECEIVED count mismatch: changing an amount produces an extra old-amount key and a missing new-amount key. Increasing a payment lowers current_balance_cents by that amount; outstanding_balance_cents drops only until its zero floor. The finding omits chapter_expenses, another mutable operational input to chapter balance. LedgerWriter.invalidate is indeed called only by tests, but direct owner SQL

primary.title: Authorization repeatedly reloads the same role and permission set within one request
primary.evidence: Every `get_member_permissions` call reads `member_roles` and `role_permissions` (`permissions.py:46-54`). `has_permission` always invokes it again (`57-65`). `/api/rbac/me/permissions` resolves permissions and then separately rereads role keys (`roles.py:28-35`). The member dashboard can call `has_permission` twice (`balances.py:58-61`), and outbox list/retry runs a dependency permission check followed by another inline check (`announcements.py:95-124`).
primary.current_behavior: There is no request-scoped permission cache. A simple roster read costs one auth query, two permission queries, and one roster query. `/me/permissions` costs four queries including auth. Branches that check two alternative permissions can spend four permission queries for the same actor.
primary.why_it_matters: Permission resolution is on nearly every startup endpoint, amplifying the 15 + 3N frontend fan-out and consuming connections without changing results during a request.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. The SPA launches its startup requests. 2. Each independently loads the member row and permissions. 3. A treasury or outbox endpoint checks more than one capability and repeats both RBAC reads. 4. The per-instance connection pool and event loop spend much of startup repeating immutable request-local data.
primary.blast_radius: Nearly every authenticated API request; greatest during SPA startup and officer workflows.
primary.tests_detect: partial — `tests/rbac/test_permissions_service.py` validates permission semantics, but no test asserts query counts or reuse. Route tests do not detect repeated resolution.
primary.recommendation: Resolve an immutable `ActorContext` once per request containing the member, role keys, and permission set. Make `require_permission` and inline ownership checks consume that context; have `/me/permissions` return the already-resolved roles and keys.

primary.title: Every in-app announcement creates a guaranteed failed delivery row
primary.evidence: The announcement RPC inserts one `ANNOUNCEMENT_PUBLISHED` row with `member_id = NULL` and a TODO saying audience fan-out is deferred. The drain explicitly turns every recipient-less row into `failed` with `last_error='no member_id (no recipient)'`. Actual feed audience filtering is implemented separately in Python, including `is_officer`.
primary.current_behavior: Posting an announcement succeeds in the feed, but its companion outbox row always fails. Retrying it repeats the same deterministic failure. The advertised delivery-time audience resolution never occurs.
primary.why_it_matters: Operators accumulate false failures and cannot distinguish expected feed markers from genuine notification outages. Officers-only audience resolution works for the feed and manual SMS, but not for this automatic email event.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. An officer sends an announcement to `officers`. 2. The RPC commits the feed post and a recipient-less outbox row. 3. Cron claims the row. 4. The drain marks it failed without resolving officers. 5. The outbox UI shows a failure; Retry can never succeed.
primary.blast_radius: One permanent failed row for every sent announcement, for every audience type.
primary.tests_detect: yes, but codifies the defect — tests/cron/test_drain_outbox.py::test_row_without_member_is_failed_not_stranded expects this failure. Announcement feed audience tests cover the separate in-app path.
primary.recommendation: Either remove `ANNOUNCEMENT_PUBLISHED` from the delivery outbox and treat the announcement table as the feed, or fan out per-member email rows atomically at send time. Do not represent an intentional non-delivery as failed.

primary.title: The PostgREST compatibility parser silently drops unsupported nested joins
primary.evidence: `FK_MAP` supports only six base tables (`postgres.py:30-37`). `_parse_select` matches every `table(columns)` expression but executes `if tbl not in fk_info: continue` (`198-201`), removing that expression from the base column list without raising. The fines adapter explicitly performs separate member/event reads because `unpaid_invoices` is not registered (`fines_legacy.py:77-101`).
primary.current_behavior: A developer can write a syntactically valid Supabase-style nested select for an unregistered relation and receive base rows with the nested field silently absent. The shim's missing joins also force manual stitching and extra queries in services.
primary.why_it_matters: The abstraction looks general but has a small hard-coded relationship catalog. Silent degradation is more dangerous than an unsupported-operation error and encourages per-domain workarounds.

The query succeeds and returns invoice rows without `members`. 4. Response code treats missing nested data as an empty/default state rather than exposing the unsupported query.

primary.tests_detect: no — no query-builder test was found asserting that an unsupported nested join raises. Existing callers work around missing mappings manually.
primary.recommendation: Fail fast on every unrecognized nested relation. Longer term, replace the emulation with explicit SQL/repository queries for complex reads while retaining a small typed CRUD helper only where it is genuinely simpler.

primary.title: Concurrent security assignment can create duplicate active shifts for one member/event
primary.evidence: `ev_assign_security` performs an unlocked `IF EXISTS` across tasks and commitments at lines 247-255, then creates a new task and commitment. The schema has only a non-unique index on security tasks; no constraint represents one active security assignment per member/event.

primary.why_it_matters: The same member can appear twice in security staffing, receive duplicate notifications, and accrue distorted prior-security-shift scoring after approval.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. Two supervisors assign the same member to security on the same event concurrently. 2. Both transactions query before either inserts. 3. Both see no assignment. 4. Each creates a security task, commitment, log, audit row, and outbox notification.

primary.title: Event-role dedup keys suppress notifications after a real remove/reassign cycle

Thus N upcoming events produce 15 + 3N HTTP calls. Every backend query executes synchronous psycopg2 on the async handler thread (`postgres.py:169-186`). Job refetches also always request both tasks and events (`useAppData.ts:104-109`).

primary.failure_scenario: 1. A 100-member chapter has 20 upcoming events. 2. An officer opens the app. 3. The browser dispatches 75 requests. 4. Each request independently authenticates and many independently resolve permissions. 5. The backend serializes substantial portions through blocking calls, causing slow startup or transient failures; failed event enrichments silently leave partial cards.
primary.blast_radius: Every authenticated SPA load; officers incur the heaviest payload because their optional endpoints succeed rather than cheaply 403.
primary.tests_detect: no — frontend unit tests cover pure adapters/helpers, not an integration-level request budget or duplicate-fetch assertion.

primary.blast_radius: Production availability detection for the entire backend.

primary.title: Concurrent chair removals can leave an initiative with zero chairs
primary.evidence: The RPC locks only the target chair row, then separately counts chairs. With two chairs, concurrent removals lock different rows and each can observe `v_remaining = 2`. There is no initiative-row lock or database minimum-cardinality constraint.
primary.current_behavior: The last-chair check works sequentially but is vulnerable to write skew. Two chairs can remove one another concurrently and both commits can succeed, leaving no actor authorized by chair membership to manage the initiative.
primary.why_it_matters: An initiative can become administratively orphaned, blocking normal updates and chair management.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. Initiative has chairs A and B. 2. A requests removal of B while B requests removal of A. 3. Each locks a different target row and counts two visible chairs. 4. Both delete. 5. The initiative has zero chairs.
primary.blast_radius: Any initiative with exactly two chairs, including its jobs and approval authority.
primary.tests_detect: No. `tests/initiatives/test_initiatives_rpcs.py` covers sequential co-chair removal and sequential rejection of removing the sole chair.
primary.recommendation: Lock the parent initiative row before authorization/count/removal so chair mutations serialize. Recheck actor membership and remaining count after acquiring the common lock.

primary.title: Any authenticated member can permanently append unbounded usage data
primary.evidence: POST `/api/usage/track` requires authentication but no permission or rate limit. The schema accepts arbitrary metadata. The service truncates each serialized payload only above 8,000 bytes, then inserts one row per request. The database trigger blocks every UPDATE and DELETE, and no retention/partitioning path exists.

primary.why_it_matters: A low-privilege account can drive database storage/cost and degrade queries until the chapter or database is deleted. Arbitrary metadata also creates an uncontrolled PII retention surface.
primary.failure_scenario: 1. A member authenticates normally. 2. A script repeatedly POSTs 8 KB metadata to `/api/usage/track`. 3. Each request appends a row. 4. Operators cannot delete or compact rows because the trigger rejects deletion. 5. Storage and index size grow until service or billing impact occurs.
primary.blast_radius: The shared database and every chapter using it; usage summaries also become increasingly expensive.
primary.tests_detect: partial — tests/calendar_view/test_usage_instrumentation.py verifies per-row truncation and explicitly verifies UPDATE/DELETE rejection, but has no rate-limit, quota, retention, or abuse test.
primary.recommendation: Remove the public generic tracker or restrict it to a closed event catalog. Add per-member rate limits, chapter quotas, metadata allowlists, and a privileged retention/pruning mechanism instead of universal immutability.

findings.lead_note: Lead downgrades to P2 (abuse/perf, not correctness). Refuter (Gemini) upgraded to P1 and added a real fact: the usage_events immutability trigger (0140:28-40) also blocks cascaded chapter/member deletes. Lead keeps P2: no delete feature exists yet.

good_patterns.title: Money rejects non-integers at construction
good_patterns.detail: Money.__init__ rejects bool and every non-int, and from_numeric rejects float and converts through Decimal with ROUND_HALF_UP. Ledger, invoice, and payment columns are BIGINT cents. Do not replace this with a float dollars field on the way into RPCs.

good_patterns.title: A verified payment cannot be created twice for one submission
good_patterns.detail: Both verify functions take the submission FOR UPDATE, return the existing row when status is already approved, and insert verified_payments under UNIQUE(submission_id). Keep that pair. Removing either the lock or the unique index reopens a double credit.

good_patterns.title: v2 invoice status is derived from coverage
good_patterns.detail: tr_invoice_remaining_cents and tr_refresh_invoice_status recompute unpaid, partially_paid, and paid from direct verified payments plus net allocation rows, and leave cancelled rows alone. Allocations are append-only (reversal rows, not updates). The unversioned v1 verify path is the exception, not the model.

good_patterns.title: Append-only triggers on the financial and audit logs
good_patterns.detail: big_ledger allows only active to invalidated with every money column unchanged. audit_logs, the commitment log, receipts, allocations, and evidence block update and delete. The fines table blocks insert, update, and delete. These triggers fire for the table owner, which is the role the app uses, so they are the real guard. Do not disable them to make a test cleanup easier.

good_patterns.title: Setup-code redeem is a single conditional update
good_patterns.detail: au_consume_setup_code updates used_at only where it is null and expires_at is in the future, and flips invited to active in the same function. A lost race returns claimed=false. Login itself requires status active (auth.py:228), so an invited row cannot get a token by email.

good_patterns.title: Job parent exclusivity and claim capacity are in the database
good_patterns.detail: tasks_single_parent_check forbids both event_id and initiative_id. tk_commit_task locks the task row, counts active commitments, and raises job_full at people_needed. A partial unique index allows only one active commitment per task and member. The security kind cannot be committed or uncommitted through tk_*; swaps move the commitment inside ev_accept_security_swap under the same row lock.

good_patterns.title: One SMS consent predicate, and the two blast types are pinned to the sms channel
good_patterns.detail: has_consent is sms_consent_at set and sms_opted_out_at null. The drain and _dispatch_twilio_row both call it before a real send. outbox_pin_sms_channel forces channel sms for ANNOUNCEMENT_SMS and EVENT_NOTIFY on insert, so a plpgsql producer cannot silently fall through to email. The duplicate-delivery race is in who sends, not in this predicate.

good_patterns.title: Standing and contribution do not import each other
good_patterns.detail: derive_standing's parameters are only unpaid_count, unpaid_total_cents, and unexcused. contribution does not import memberadmin and memberadmin does not import contribution. The engagement score is a separate officer-gated function and is the ADR-0004 exception. The bug is the data fed into those three parameters, not a second formula hiding task counts. Do not fold contribution into derive_standing.

weird_but_reasonable.title: BalanceEngine never reads big_ledger
weird_but_reasonable.detail: Member balance is unpaid invoice amounts minus verified payments plus signed adjustments plus refunds. The ledger is a shadow the rebuild compares. That split is deliberate: a bad ledger row cannot move a balance, and a balance bug cannot be hidden by editing history. The cache is the part that drifts, not this formula.

weird_but_reasonable.title: v2 verify allocates oldest-first and ignores the submission's invoice_id
weird_but_reasonable.detail: The service docstring says leftover becomes member credit and coverage is oldest-first. A payment submitted against one invoice can close an older fine. That matches the allocation design. The unversioned v1 route is the conflicting writer, not this order.

weird_but_reasonable.title: Security swap acceptance does not call tk_commit_task
weird_but_reasonable.detail: tk_commit_task and tk_uncommit_task raise on kind=security. ev_accept_security_swap updates the commitment rows itself under FOR UPDATE so the guards cannot reject the swap. Copying that SQL into a second path would be the bug; this duplication is the lock.

weird_but_reasonable.title: The query builder inlines the string now() as SQL NOW()
weird_but_reasonable.detail: Every other filter value is a parameter, so a date column compared to the text now() would not call the clock. The special case is what makes engagement's filter run. The standing bug is comparing a DATE to that clock, not the special case itself.

weird_but_reasonable.title: LEGACY_ROLE_COMPAT still unions members.role into permissions
weird_but_reasonable.detail: Pre-0154 promotions wrote only the column. The union keeps those accounts working, and mem_set_legacy_role writes both sides on the legacy PUT. That dual read is justified. The hole is rbac_revoke_role, which updates only one side.

(3) BYPASS: the reset path inserts the code and bumps in two autocommit statements, so a failed bump leaves a live code and live old sessions. (5) TESTS: tests/auth/test_tokens.py, test_invite_setup_codes.py. (6) strong for password change and for a completed reset bump.

extra.title: A setup code is single-use and expires
extra.detail: (1) ENFORCED: au_consume_setup_code updates only a row with used_at null and expires_at in the future. The route also checks expiry and the hash before calling it. au_invite_member inserts the member and the code in one function. (2) ASSUMED: redeem maps claimed=false to the same 401 as a bad code. (3) BYPASS: several unused unexpired codes can exist (invite plus later resets); each is independently redeemable until used. Hash check is outside the RPC, so a caller who can execute the function with a code id consumes it without the secret. 0153 revokes PUBLIC and anon/authenticated; the app role still can. (4) DB: the conditional UPDATE. No unique on the hash. (5) TESTS: tests/auth/test_invite_setup_codes.py, test_rpc_privileges.py. (6) strong for the HTTP redeem path.

extra.title: An invited member cannot log in by email alone
extra.detail: (1) ENFORCED: login and dev-login both require status=active. Invited rows are created by au_invite_member. Consume flips invited to active only after a valid code. Passwordless active members still do not receive a token from login; they get 401 or 403. (2) ASSUMED: the invite flow's comment. (3) BYPASS: redeem of a valid code returns a 7-day token before a password is set. That is the code working, not email-only login. (4) DB: members status check includes invited. (5) TESTS: tests/auth/test_login_password.py, test_invite_setup_codes.py. (6) strong.

extra.title: Attendance has at most one row per event and member, and status transitions are guarded
extra.detail: (1) ENFORCED: UNIQUE (event_id, member_id). at_set_attendance upserts checked_in and, for excused, replaces the excuse; for absent, deletes excuses. There is no status column; S2's present/absent/excused/late check does not exist in 0001. (2) ASSUMED: roster and standing treat checked_in as present and an approved excuse as excused. (3) BYPASS: link and phone check-in upsert checked_in=true and do not delete an approved excuse, so both can stand. They write no audit row. Phone check-in uses data[0] when the phone matches several members. The present branch of at_set_attendance also leaves excuses in place. (4) DB: the unique constraint and method check (manual|link). No transition trigger. (5) TESTS: tests/attendance/test_tenant_guards.py for the RPC rollback. (6) partial — one row is strong; the excused/present relationship is not a guarded transition on the check-in paths.

extra.title: An approved excuse and a fine for the same event and member cannot both stand
extra.detail: (1) ENFORCED: excuses UNIQUE (event_id, member_id). at_review_excuse voids one unpaid kind=fine invoice for that pair. (2) ASSUMED: the 0146 comment says approving an excuse waives the fine. (3) BYPASS: at_set_attendance excused creates the approved excuse and does not void. Review skips partially_paid and any fine after the first unpaid. A fine issued after the excuse, through the generic invoice route or a race, is not cleared. Check-in does not void a fine already issued. (4) DB: excuse uniqueness only. No exclusion constraint with unpaid_invoices. (5) TESTS: test_approve_after_fine_processing_voids_the_invoice. (6) weak.

extra.title: Standing derives only from unpaid fines and unexcused absences
extra.detail: (1) ENFORCED: derive_standing takes only those three numbers. standing.py does not import tasks or contribution. The engagement score is a separate officer-only route and does not call derive_standing. (2) ASSUMED: ADR-0004 and the firewall test, which check the parameter names. (3) BYPASS: the numbers themselves are wrong. Unexcused includes required events whose date is today but whose time has not passed. Unpaid fines are status=unpaid at full amount_cents, so partially_paid fines disappear and reallocation can recreate them. Contribution is not an input. (4) DB: none; standing is computed. (5) TESTS: test_standing_firewall.py, test_standing_rules.py, test_engagement_fines.py. (6) partial — the formula is firewalled; the inputs are not the absences and the amounts owed.

extra.title: A task has at most one of event or initiative, and active commitments never exceed people_needed
extra.detail: (1) ENFORCED: CHECK (event_id IS NULL OR initiative_id IS NULL). tk_create_task raises task_two_parents. tk_commit_task locks the task, counts active rows, and raises job_full. Partial unique index on active (task_id, member_id). tk_update_task refuses people_needed below the active count. Security tasks require an event (tasks_security_event_check) and people_needed 1 at assign time. (2) ASSUMED: the jobs UI capacity display. (3) BYPASS: create_task sets people_needed in a follow-up autocommit UPDATE when it is not 1, after the row exists at the default 1. That window only lowers capacity, it does not raise claims over the final number. None (both parents null) is allowed, which matches the stated rule. (4) DB: the check, the partial unique index, people_needed >= 1. (5) TESTS: task commitment tests in tests/tasks. (6) strong.

extra.title: Security swap transitions are a closed state machine
extra.detail: (1) ENFORCED: status check pending|accepted|declined|cancelled. One pending row per task (partial unique index). ev_enforce_swap_update blocks any change after the row leaves pending, and blocks changes to the identity columns while pending. Accept checks the actor is the target, the task is in_progress security, and the requester's commitment is still active, then flips the commitment in the same function. Python only calls the ev_* RPCs. (2) ASSUMED: the swap UI. (3) BYPASS: the trigger does not constrain which terminal status is written, so a direct UPDATE from pending to accepted would mark the swap resolved without moving the commitment. No application path does that. (4) DB: check, partial unique index, update and delete triggers. (5) TESTS: tests/events/test_security.py. (6) strong for the application; the transition graph lives in the RPCs.

extra.title: An outbox row is sent at most once, and SMS goes only to consented members
extra.detail: (1) ENFORCED: UNIQUE(dedup_key) on insert. Claim uses FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, sets sending, and increments attempts. Drain and _dispatch_twilio_row both refuse a real SMS when has_consent is false. The pin trigger forces the two blast types onto channel sms. (2) ASSUMED: ADR-0005's exactly-once wording in outbox.py. (3) BYPASS: delivery is at-least-once. Status is updated in a later autocommit after Twilio or SMTP returns. The reaper returns sending to pending after 15 minutes. dispatch_send and the cron both send the same pending SMS rows. Consent is not checked inside an_send_announcement_sms; it trusts the id list and rechecks at send time. (4) DB: unique dedup_key and status check. No 'sent is terminal and irreversible' constraint beyond the application. (5) TESTS: tests/cron/test_drain_outbox.py including the consent and reaper cases; test_sms_send.py. No double-sender test. (6) partial — enqueue dedup and the consent predicate are strong; single delivery is not.

extra.title: Idempotency keys make retried mutations no-ops
extra.detail: (1) ENFORCED: UNIQUE (chapter_id, operation, key). Each RPC returns the stored jsonb result when the key exists. (2) ASSUMED: clients that reuse a key expect the same effect. (3) BYPASS: the payload is not hashed, so a second body with the same key returns the first result. Keys do not expire. A null key skips the check; process_event_fines and at_set_attendance's route pass null. Different operation names (create_invoice vs create_invoice_v2, verify_payment vs verify_payment_v2) do not dedupe each other. The stored result is the row at insert time, so a later void does not change what a replay returns. (4) DB: the unique index only. (5) TESTS: treasury idempotency tests. (6) partial — retries of the same key are stable; they are not proof the body matched.

extra.title: Every trust-boundary mutation goes through an RPC that writes audit_logs
extra.detail: (1) ENFORCED: money RPCs, rbac_assign/revoke, mem_set_legacy_role, at_set_attendance, at_review_excuse, tk_* lifecycle, ev_* swaps, an_send_*, and au_invite_member. (2) ASSUMED: CLAUDE.md's hard rule. (3) BYPASS, Python writers outside platform/ that this pass grepped: auth.py member_setup_codes insert and login_attempts insert; payments.py payment_evidence insert; ledger.py big_ledger insert/update (tests); tasks/services/templates.py event_tasks insert and events update; tasks/services/tasks.py tasks.people_needed update; recruitment pipeline insert; members.py sms consent update; usage_events insert; nl_controller command insert/update; events/services/events.py event_types and events update; outbox.py message_outbox insert; outbox_drain.py and sms.py and announcements outbox status updates; chapters onboarding members.sms_consent_at update; bylaws insert; attendance sessions insert and events.linked_attendance_session_id update; checkin_links insert and active update; excuses delete+insert; attendance upsert on both check-in routes; twilio_inbound members update by phone; announcements insert/delete/hide; balance.py member_finance_accounts upsert; audit.py audit_logs insert (tests). Check-in and excuse submit write no audit row. (4) DB: audit insert is per function, not a general trigger. (5) TESTS: per-RPC audit assertions in treasury and attendance tenant tests. No test that check-in writes audit_logs. (6) partial — financial and role writes match the rule; attendance check-in, excuse submit, consent, and outbox delivery do not.

extra.title: Migrations are never edited after apply
extra.detail: (1) ENFORCED: scripts/migrate_db.py records the filename and skips it. Nothing detects a content change. (2) ASSUMED: CLAUDE.md and the migration comments. (3) BYPASS: 0147 and 0149 were committed twice. The second commit changes behavior, and both files say a database that already ran them keeps the first behavior. 0159's second commit only adds REVOKE on outbox_pin_sms_channel; the passing privilege test implies the demo database has that revoke now. 0080 has one commit. (4) DB: schema_migrations primary key is the filename. (5) TESTS: none. (6) absent — the rule is documentation; 0147 and 0149 violate it on purpose, with leftover treasurer grants and wiped phones on the database the comments name.

extra.title: Production config cannot boot with dev defaults
extra.detail: (1) ENFORCED: production_config_violations runs at import when VERCEL_ENV is production or preview. It rejects a short or local-dev JWT_SECRET, empty DATABASE_URL, DEV_AUTH_BYPASS, a short CRON_SECRET, localhost FRONTEND_URL, and incomplete Twilio or SMTP settings. dev-login 404s when is_deployed. (2) ASSUMED: a booted production process is not the demo configuration. (3) BYPASS: the guard does not compare DATABASE_URL to the demo project ref, so a production boot whose URL is the demo pooler still starts. PLATFORM_SECRET and TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS are not checked. Local VERCEL_ENV empty skips the guard entirely. (4) DB: none. (5) TESTS: config/boot tests if present were not re-run; the function was read in full. (6) partial — the known dev secrets are refused on a deploy; pointing production at the demo database is not.

good_patterns.title: Atomic task claiming and lifecycle mutations
good_patterns.detail: `tk_commit_task` locks the task before capacity calculation, preventing ordinary double-claim races. Report/approve/reject RPCs lock task state and write commitments, audit, and outbox effects transactionally. Preserve this RPC boundary when repairing the generic status route.

good_patterns.title: Security swap acceptance has strong transactional guards
good_patterns.detail: Acceptance locks the swap and task, verifies target identity, current state, requester ownership, and target conflicts, then flips commitments and enqueues notifications atomically. This complexity is justified and should not be decomposed into Python writes.

good_patterns.title: Event visibility is consistently reused by calendar and event detail
good_patterns.detail: Chapter/officer/custom visibility, supervisor access, organizer access, and officer-view permission are enforced in the shared event service. Calendar calls that service rather than rebuilding weaker visibility logic.

good_patterns.title: Contribution and standing are structurally firewalled
good_patterns.detail: Contribution is derived read-only from existing rows and is intentionally excluded from standing. The AST/signature tests are narrow but effective at preventing accidental participation quotas; preserve this policy while fixing engagement aggregation.

good_patterns.title: Notification audience privacy and outbox deduplication
good_patterns.detail: Automatic creation emails are limited to chapter-visible events, role-assignment email distinguishes assignment from volunteering, and deterministic per-event/member dedup keys make retries safe. The helpers also avoid rolling back the primary mutation on email failure.

weird_but_reasonable.title: Ambiguous legacy session fallback
weird_but_reasonable.detail: The bound-session/unbound-open-session resolution is complex because the foreign key lives on the session side and older links may predate binding. The compatibility fallback is understandable; the unsafe part is failing open on ambiguity, not the existence of the fallback itself.

weird_but_reasonable.title: Roll call intentionally permits partial success
weird_but_reasonable.detail: The frontend uses `Promise.allSettled` so one rejected member does not discard the rest of a large roll call, then names failed members for re-entry. This is a defensible UX over per-member endpoints, though an atomic bulk RPC would ultimately be cleaner.

weird_but_reasonable.title: Commitment history uses append-only log plus mutable current row
weird_but_reasonable.detail: Separating current commitment state from an append-only action log looks redundant but supports accountability, late-unclaim attribution, and security swap history. Preserve the log when consolidating task APIs.

conventions.dominant: Database SELECT results retain native UUID objects; many services normalize IDs with `str(...)` before set/map comparison.
conventions.competing: Several authorization branches directly compare body/path strings with raw current-user UUIDs.
conventions.recommendation: Canonicalize IDs at the dependency/data-access boundary and prohibit direct mixed-type identity comparisons.

conventions.dominant: Modern trust-boundary workflows use atomic plpgsql RPCs with locks, tenant checks, idempotency rows, audit, and outbox writes.
conventions.competing: Event update, check-in/session creation, template application, and task capacity still compose autocommitted query-builder operations in Python.
conventions.recommendation: Use RPCs whenever one logical command changes multiple rows or requires a cross-row invariant.

conventions.dominant: Active UI, event completeness, commitments, approvals, security, initiatives, and contribution use `tasks`.
conventions.competing: The mounted operations engine uses `event_tasks`/`event_roles` with a separate status model and no frontend lifecycle.
conventions.recommendation: Migrate templates/readiness to `tasks` and retire the shadow model.

conventions.dominant: Frontend inputs and display treat event date/time as local wall time.
conventions.competing: Fine eligibility explicitly treats them as UTC, task RPCs use database-session timezone, and standing uses date only.
conventions.recommendation: Adopt an explicit chapter timezone and canonical event/initiative start instant shared by every layer.

extra.title: event create/update/cancel workflow
extra.detail: Create: EVENT_CREATE dependency -> schema/range validation -> `ev_create_event`, atomically inserting event, creator supervisor, audience, audit, and idempotency result -> best-effort creation email. Update: EVENT_UPDATE -> direct scalar update -> optional `ev_set_audience`; missing atomicity described above. Cancel does not exist; DELETE physically removes the event and collides with dependent FK/append-only behavior.

extra.title: audience and visibility workflow
extra.detail: List/detail first chapter-scope events, then allow chapter visibility; officer visibility via `calendar:officer:view`; custom membership; or supervisor/organizer association. Audience replacement validates member chapter in `ev_set_audience`. Missing guard: scalar visibility update and audience replacement are not one transaction.

extra.title: organizers and supervisors workflow
extra.detail: Creator is auto-added and locked as supervisor; minimum-one supervisor is enforced in RPC. Organizers support self-volunteer or EVENT_UPDATE assignment and idempotent DB uniqueness. Missing guard: Python self/other decisions compare mixed UUID/string types; target active status is not consistently required.

extra.title: event notification workflow
extra.detail: Supervisor/organizer/EVENT_UPDATE -> preview completeness and chapter SMS recipients -> frontend confirms recipient count -> service re-resolves count -> RPC rechecks completeness/cooldown, inserts send/audit/outbox atomically -> dispatcher sends. Missing guard: cooldown check is not serialized; count confirmation does not itself prevent concurrent duplicate sends.

extra.title: check-in link and session workflow
extra.detail: CHECKIN_CREATE -> event chapter check -> deactivate old links -> insert random-code link with five collision retries -> optionally bind open sessions. Public validation checks active+TTL and one resolved session's closes_at. Missing invariants: one active link/event, one governing session/link, atomic link+session+event pointer creation, and fail-closed ambiguity.

extra.title: public and authenticated check-in workflow
extra.detail: `/c/{code}` renders a phone form; phone POST validates code/session, normalizes phone, finds the first active same-chapter member, rejects an existing checked-in row, and upserts attendance with method=link. Authenticated POST uses JWT member identity and chapter match. Both are idempotent only through a pre-read plus unique upsert, and neither reconciles an existing excuse.

extra.title: manual roll-call workflow
extra.detail: Frontend issues one request per member with `Promise.allSettled`. ATTENDANCE_OVERRIDE -> atomic `at_set_attendance`: validates event/member/actor tenant and active status, upserts attendance, mutates excuse state, and audits. Each member is atomic, but the roster is intentionally partial-commit; no request idempotency key is supplied.

extra.title: attendance summary and absence signals
extra.detail: Summary enforces self-or-officer read access and derives checked-in percentage across required events. `list_unexcused_absences` subtracts checked-in and approved-excused members; the fine route separately validates required event and timing. Missing guard: both summary and engagement use date-level rather than completed-event eligibility.

extra.title: excuse workflow
extra.detail: Authenticated member submits only for self and same-chapter event; pending/approved duplicates conflict, denied rows are deleted then replaced. EXCUSE_REVIEW -> `at_review_excuse`, which tenant-locks the excuse, writes decision/audit, and voids one matching unpaid fine on approval. Missing transitions: submit-after-check-in, review only from pending, and compensation for a reversed approval.

extra.title: standing and scoring workflow
extra.detail: Active members -> required-event attendance/approved excuses + unpaid fine invoices -> missed count -> standing thresholds: warning at one fine or absence; delinquent at two fines, $50, or three absences. Standing is dynamically derived, not cached. Defects: fines skipped when there are zero required events and current-day events counted before start.

extra.title: contribution record workflow
extra.detail: Chapter-scoped member validation -> organizer/supervisor event records, initiative chairs, approved committed jobs, and checked-in count -> read-only response. It does not mutate or feed standing. The standing firewall is structural and currently holds.

extra.title: calendar workflow
extra.detail: Calendar reuses visible event listing, adds chapter initiatives and chapter-audience sent announcements, then invoice/task due dates. Event visibility is preserved. Date boundaries default from UTC while frontend month/day uses browser-local dates, another symptom of the missing chapter-timezone model.

extra.title: task/job state machine
extra.detail: Intended states: open -> in_progress on first commit -> done_reported via `tk_report_done` -> approved via `tk_approve_task`, or back to in_progress via `tk_reject_task`; cancel only for eligible unclaimed jobs. Generic `tk_update_task_status` independently allows open/committed/in_progress/done/cancelled from almost any source state, bypassing the intended machine.

extra.title: commitment state machine
extra.detail: No commitment -> active through task-row-locked capacity check -> uncommitted via T-36 guard, or completed when task is done/approved. Recommit after uncommit is supported; append-only log records every action. Missing guards: active member status and canonical identity comparison at HTTP self/other authorization.

extra.title: security assignment state machine
extra.detail: Assignment creates security task in_progress + active commitment + log/audit/outbox. Report/approve/reject reuse the job lifecycle. Removal cancels pending swap, uncommits holder, logs, and cancels task; approved assignments cannot be removed. Missing invariant: concurrent assignment can violate one active security shift per member/event; target need not be active.

extra.title: security swap state machine
extra.detail: pending is created only by current holder, self-target and already-assigned target are rejected, and a partial unique index permits one pending swap/task. Target alone may accept/decline; requester may cancel. Accept locks swap+task, rechecks holder and target conflict, atomically flips commitments, resolves swap, and notifies parties/supervisors. Resolved rows are immutable. Missing guard: target active status is not checked at request or acceptance.

extra.title: initiative and chair state machine
extra.detail: CALENDAR_INITIATIVE_CREATE -> atomic initiative creation with creator chair and optional co-chairs. Assigned chairs can update, add, or remove chairs; DB uniqueness makes duplicate add idempotent; last-chair removal is rejected sequentially. Missing serialization allows two-chair write skew to zero chairs.

extra.title: templates and operations state machine
extra.detail: GET templates -> POST apply loops through legacy roles/tasks and patches event defaults -> GET readiness counts legacy event_tasks statuses. There is no exposed transition endpoint for those task statuses and no frontend call site. This state machine is disconnected from active `tasks` commitments and approvals.

extra.title: time interpretation matrix
extra.detail: Frontend entry/countdowns use browser-local dates and local `Date`; fine eligibility explicitly treats naive event fields as UTC; task uncommit uses database-session timezone; attendance/standing discard time entirely; calendar defaults its range in UTC. No chapter timezone unifies these interpretations.

good_patterns.title: JWT verification pins algorithm, issuer, and audience
good_patterns.detail: Decode allows only HS256 and requires exp, sub, aud, and iss, all set to guildos. Pre-hardening tokens without those claims die. ver is checked against members.token_version on every request. Do not relax algorithms or make ver optional.

good_patterns.title: Setup codes are stored as bcrypt and redacted in the outbox view
good_patterns.detail: Only the hash is inserted. Log lines from a failed enqueue scrub the code. Officer outbox rendering replaces SETUP_CODE and RESET_CODE bodies with a fixed string and does not return the payload column. Keep that filter if the list response is ever changed to return the row.

good_patterns.title: Cron, platform, and Twilio secrets fail closed with constant-time compare
good_patterns.detail: Empty CRON_SECRET is 401, not open. A wrong PLATFORM_SECRET is 401 rather than falling through to the public signup path. Twilio rejects when TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN is unset and signs BASE_URL plus the path, not the attacker Host header. Sentry sets include_local_variables=False because frames can hold SMTP passwords and setup codes. No cookie auth exists, so CORS allow_credentials does not create a CSRF channel for the bearer token.

good_patterns.title: Check-in HTML escapes officer-controlled event text
good_patterns.detail: Title, date, and location go through html.escape in markup and _js_literal (json.dumps plus <, >, &, U+2028/U+2029) inside the script. Success text is assigned with textContent. tests/attendance/test_checkin_page_escaping.py exists for this. Do not interpolate event fields raw if the page is redesigned.

good_patterns.title: IDOR-prone mutations that were checked do validate the other id inside the RPC
good_patterns.detail: Manual attendance requires event, member, and actor to be active in p_chapter_id, and p_chapter_id comes from the session. Initiative create rejects chair UUIDs that are not in the chapter before insert. Swap request rejects a target member outside the chapter. Evidence GET filters payment_evidence and the parent submission by the caller's chapter_id and then requires owner or treasury:payment:verify. Link check-in compares both chapter ids from SELECT rows (both uuid.UUID), so that particular check is not the string/UUID bug.

weird_but_reasonable.title: is_officer is every catalog role except member
weird_but_reasonable.detail: NON_OFFICER_ROLE_KEYS is only {member}, so treasury_viewer and alumni_advisor count as officers for announcement audiences. The comment says audience membership must match authorization. Both sides of the member-id dict in the SMS path are SELECT UUIDs, so that lookup matches. Narrow roles seeing officer-only blasts is the documented tradeoff, not an accident.

weird_but_reasonable.title: require_permission is ANY-of
weird_but_reasonable.detail: Multiple keys mean the caller needs one of them. The NL list route uses execute OR approve on purpose. Do not flip the helper to ALL-of without revisiting every call site.

weird_but_reasonable.title: Chapter signup limiter is deliberately in-process
weird_but_reasonable.detail: The comment states the ceiling is workers times the limit and that it stops a script, not a botnet. That is an honest bound. The X-Forwarded-For issue is separate: the bound is only real when a single trusted proxy appends the client.

weird_but_reasonable.title: PUT demotion intentionally leaves stackable roles
weird_but_reasonable.detail: mem_set_legacy_role deletes only the officer member_roles row so treasurer and similar grants survive. The test pins that. It is reasonable. It becomes dangerous only because officer includes roles:assign, which can attach admin before the demotion, and because the DELETE role path does not clear the legacy column.

conventions.dominant: require_permission(*keys) as a FastAPI dependency before the handler body; chapter id taken from the user dict, not the body
conventions.competing: Inline has_permission after a load (balances, statements, evidence, excuses list, task status, announcement drafts) and chair/supervisor checks that ignore the seeded permission key
conventions.recommendation: Keep the dependency for new routes. When a check is ownership-based, compare str() ids and put it next to the load, as payments evidence does.

conventions.dominant: str(a) == str(b) on treasury ownership and roster consent
conventions.competing: Raw == / != / in against user['id'] from SELECT (uuid.UUID) and path or JSON strings (commit, organizer, attendance summary)
conventions.recommendation: One helper used at every Python compare. SQL .eq() is fine because the driver casts.

conventions.dominant: Session chapter_id passed into an RPC that re-checks every referenced id
conventions.competing: Python filters after a global select (event templates, roster email lookup, fine name stitching) and legacy writes that rely on a derive trigger (excuse insert, link check-in)

good_patterns.title: Atomic RPC-side producers preserve business mutation, audit, and outbox consistency
good_patterns.detail: Announcement SMS, event notify, and job/security lifecycle RPCs validate tenant references and write domain state, audit rows, and outbox rows in one PostgreSQL transaction. Preserve this boundary; moving these writes back into sequential Python calls would reintroduce partial commits.

good_patterns.title: Claim protocol correctly excludes overlapping cron workers and recovers abandoned claims
good_patterns.detail: `UPDATE ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` atomically claims rows, records attempts, reaps stale claims, and caps poison rows. Tests cover worker exclusion, stale recovery, and attempt caps. The flaw is the separate inline dispatcher, not the claim RPC itself.

good_patterns.title: SMS consent has one definition and is enforced at preview and both real-send boundaries
good_patterns.detail: Twilio-mode previews exclude unconsented members, and both inline and cron delivery re-check consent immediately before sending. Every SMS body receives a STOP footer. Keep this centralized rule and defense-in-depth check.

good_patterns.title: Email templates are plain text and credential/error surfaces are deliberately redacted
good_patterns.detail: Email uses static subjects plus `EmailMessage.set_content`, so member-controlled titles/reasons are not inserted as raw HTML. Officer outbox rendering hides setup/reset bodies, treasury rows require treasury access, and auth enqueue logging scrubs plaintext codes.

good_patterns.title: Provider adapters are narrow, timeout-bounded boundaries
good_patterns.detail: All Twilio and SMTP network calls pass through one adapter each, with explicit 15/20-second timeouts and safe dry-run-gated smoke scripts. This makes replacement and targeted instrumentation straightforward.

good_patterns.title: Operational database writers use fail-closed target guards
good_patterns.detail: Migration, seed, and chapter-provision paths classify database URLs, reject unknown targets, redact connection strings, and require typed production confirmation. Extend this pattern to the break-glass password script.

weird_but_reasonable.title: Delivery uses live mode rather than the row’s historical delivery_mode
weird_but_reasonable.detail: Rows snapshot delivery mode at enqueue time, but the drain deliberately reads current MESSAGE_DELIVERY_MODE/EMAIL_DELIVERY_MODE. This permits messages queued during dry-run to deliver after activation. It is surprising but operationally useful if documented and paired with an explicit activation/review procedure.

weird_but_reasonable.title: Dry-run SMS parents are `sent` while children are `simulated`
weird_but_reasonable.detail: The parent tables have only queued/sent/failed, so dry-run completion is represented as parent `sent` plus `delivery_mode=dry_run`, while per-recipient truth is `simulated`. The distinction is defensible but UI labels must always display delivery mode to avoid implying real delivery.

weird_but_reasonable.title: Transactional email does not use SMS consent
weird_but_reasonable.detail: Email covers account, financial, assignment, and chapter-operational notices, while STOP is carrier-specific. Treating chapter membership as the transactional-email basis is coherent; adding SMS consent checks to email would incorrectly suppress core account operations.

conventions.dominant: RPC-side workflow producers atomically write business state, audit, and outbox rows.
conventions.competing: Python-side treasury, auth, and event-email producers commit business state first and enqueue best-effort afterward.
conventions.recommendation: Make the boundary explicit: critical notification producers should use atomic RPCs; intentionally best-effort notifications should return/log a typed failure rather than silently pretending dedup.

conventions.dominant: Automatic notifications use email; only ANNOUNCEMENT_SMS and EVENT_NOTIFY use SMS.
conventions.competing: The legacy `delivery_mode` column snapshots a global mode even though channel-specific live settings control delivery.
conventions.recommendation: Keep the two-channel policy, rename/split historical mode fields to `queued_sms_mode` and `queued_email_mode` or remove them where they do not govern behavior.

conventions.dominant: Runtime API/provider code reads typed `Settings`.
conventions.competing: Operational scripts read raw environment variables directly; local `.env` contains multiple ignored legacy names.
conventions.recommendation: Publish one generated environment reference from Settings metadata and explicitly classify app, test-only, migration-only, and obsolete variables.

conventions.dominant: CI installs exact `requirements.txt` and `package-lock.json` inputs.
conventions.competing: Local bootstrap accepts any importable FastAPI and any existing node_modules; Prod pins another Python set.
conventions.recommendation: Adopt one lock/sync workflow and one supported Python/Node version across local, CI, and deployment roots.

conventions.dominant: Modules use standard named loggers and caught provider errors include outbox row IDs.
conventions.competing: Only unhandled errors manually include request IDs; routine/caught logs use an uncorrelated plain-text format.
conventions.recommendation: Use structured logging with automatic request_id, chapter_id, outbox_id, and event_type fields.
